deep.reconstruction:
Setting (29.11.83, the first page of the 1983 Teichmüller notes). X is a compact oriented surface with boundary. Each boundary circle T_i (i in I = π0(∂X)) carries a 'structure torique', meaning a structure of torsor under U = {|z|=1}; this is the same as an orientation-compatible parametrization up to rotation.

Definitions.
- Aut(X) is the topological group of diffeomorphisms of X preserving the orientation and the family of torsor structures. Such a map may permute the boundary circles, but must act on them by torsor isomorphisms.
- Aut^!(X) is the subgroup inducing the identity on ∂X.
- SRT(X) := Aut(X)/Aut^!(X)_0.
- Since we only divide by the identity component of the boundary-fixing subgroup, SRT(X) is a Lie group, not a discrete group. Its identity component is R^I.

Dévissage. SRT(X) has three successive subquotients:
- S_*T^!(X) = Aut^!/Aut^!_0, the mapping class group fixing the boundary pointwise;
- U^I, the rotations of the boundary circles;
- S_I, the permutations of boundary components.
Refining via the capping/forgetful sequence 1 → Z^I → S_*T^!(X) → T^!(X) → 1 gives four layers Z^I, T^!(X), U^I, S_I. Here Z^I is generated by the boundary Dehn twists, and T^!(X) is the pure mapping class group of the surface with boundary circles replaced by punctures. T(X) denotes the non-pure version, with T(X)/T^!(X) = S_I.

The subgroup R^I. Grothendieck defines canonically a distinguished subgroup R^I ⊂ SRT(X) containing Z^I. These are the 'fractional Dehn twists': rotate a collar of T_i by a total angle 2πθ_i, interpolating to the identity inward; θ_i = 1 gives the Dehn twist. One has:
- R^I ∩ S_*T^! = Z^I;
- SRT^!(X) := ker(SRT(X) → S_I) equals R^I · S_*T^!(X).
The square Z^I → S_*T^!, Z^I → R^I, with both mapping to SRT^!, is cocartesian. Since Z^I is central in S_*T^!, this gives SRT^! = S_*T^! ×^{Z^I} R^I. The group R^I/Z^I = U^I is the rotation part.

The quotient SUT(X). Set SUT(X) := SRT(X)/Z^I. It is an extension
(*) 1 → U^I → SUT(X) → T(X) → 1
of the discrete mapping class group of the punctured surface by the torus U^I.

The NB remark. As I read it, it says SUT(X) ≅ T(X) ×_{S_I} Aut((T_i)_{i∈I}), where Aut((T_i)) ≅ U^I ⋊ S_I is the group of automorphisms of the family of torsors, permutations allowed. This is correct:
- SUT maps to Aut((T_i)) through the boundary action, which is well defined because Z^I acts trivially on ∂X;
- the kernel of the combined map to T(X) ×_{S_I} Aut((T_i)) is (Z^I)/Z^I = 1;
- the map is surjective.
So (*) is the pullback of the torus extension of S_I along T(X) → S_I.

Base points. Choosing base points s = (s_i) ∈ ∏ T_i gives an embedding S_*T(X,s) ↪ SRT(X). Here S_*T(X,s) is the mapping class group of maps that permute the boundary circles carrying s_i to s_σ(i), modulo isotopy rel boundary. Pushing out along Z^I → R^I gives S_*T(X,s) ∧^{Z^I} R^I ≅ SRT(X).

The next page interprets this further:
- s gives a splitting φ_s of (*);
- changing s by u ∈ U^I conjugates the splitting, φ_{us} = int(u)∘φ_s;
- so the subgroups S_*T(X,s) are R^I-conjugate.
The moral, stated on page 2: the base-point data s are 'non-modular', whereas SRT(X) depends only on the modular datum of the torsor structures.

Purpose. This sets up the topological (real-blow-up / tangential base point) model for the Teichmüller groups and groupoids of the Esquisse: boundary circles with U-torsor structure are the circles of tangent directions at punctures. The goal is to compare the 'surfaces with boundary' and 'punctured surfaces with tangential base points' versions of the Teichmüller tower, together with the gluing operations.
errors: No genuine mathematical error is visible. One terminological point: Grothendieck sometimes writes SRT^! for the kernel of SRT → S_I and S_*T^! for the boundary-fixing mapping class group. The cocartesian square relies on Z^I being central in S_*T^!, which holds because boundary Dehn twists commute with all boundary-fixing maps; this is implicit, not stated.

In the full (non-pure) group S_*T(X,s), Z^I is only normal (S_I permutes the factors), not central. The contracted product ∧^{Z^I} R^I therefore needs the compatible S_I-actions; Grothendieck leaves this implicit.

The fiber-product description of SUT (the NB) shows that (*) splits abstractly. One should note that the splitting depends on a choice of section S_I → Aut((T_i)), for instance one given by base points. This matches page 2, so it is not an error, but the page does not say it.

ideas.what: Mapping class group of a surface with boundary, modulo only the identity component of boundary-fixing diffeomorphisms, giving a Lie group SRT(X) with identity component R^I.
ideas.modern_name: Extended mapping class group of a surface with parametrized boundary (fractional / real Dehn twists); cf. mapping class groups in Segal-style CFT with parametrized boundary circles
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Segal's CFT axioms (c.1987-88), Moore-Seiberg (1989), Bakalov-Kirillov (2000)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses Teichmüller groupoids and surfaces with boundary, but I am unsure it contains this R^I construction explicitly

ideas.what: Dévissage SRT: Z^I, T^!(X), U^I, S_I; boundary Dehn twists central, giving the capping exact sequence 1→Z^I→Γ_{g,I bdry}→Γ_{g,I punct}^{pure}→1.
SUT(X) = SRT/Z^I as an extension of T(X) by the torus U^I, identified with the fiber product T(X) ×_{S_I} Aut((T_i)).
ideas.modern_name: Mapping class group with unit-tangent (framing) data at punctures; topological model of tangential base points
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tangential base points: Deligne (1989); topological framed versions: various

ideas.what: Choice of boundary base points s gives a splitting of (*) and an embedding S_*T(X,s) ↪ SRT(X), with SRT = S_*T(X,s) ∧^{Z^I} R^I. Changing s conjugates by lifts in R^I, so SRT depends only on the 'modular' torsor data.
ideas.modern_name: Independence of tangential base point up to conjugacy; pushout of mapping class group along Z→R
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard in spirit; not attributable to one source

missed.claim: Already in Nov. 1983, Grothendieck builds the Teichmüller tower on surfaces with boundary circles carrying U(1)-torsor ('toric') structures. Fractional Dehn twists R^I form a canonical normal subgroup, and the torus extension SUT(X) of the punctured mapping class group T(X) appears. This is essentially the structure later used for mapping class groups of surfaces with parametrized boundary in Segal/Moore–Seiberg CFT. It is also the topological counterpart of Deligne's tangential base points (1989), with the 'modular vs non-modular' distinction made explicit.
missed.quote: Soit X surf. à bord compacte orientée, à structure torique (i.e. torseur sous U = {z∈C | |z|=1}) donnée sur les comp. connexes du bord ... on définit canon. un sous-groupe distingué R^I de SRT(X) contenant Z^I
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This documents that Grothendieck's Esquisse-era Teichmüller program used a Lie-group (R^I-extended) mapping class group with boundary torsor data. That gives a precise bridge between the Grothendieck–Teichmüller tower (Hatcher–Lochak–Schneps) and the modular-functor/CFT formalism, of historical interest. The mathematics itself is not new.

deep.surprise_reason: The constructions are correct and somewhat elegant: the fiber-product description of SUT, and the canonical R^I with cocartesian square. Specialists, however, would recognize them as standard ingredients of mapping class groups with parametrized boundary. The interest is mainly historical: an early, careful 'modular' framework with toric boundary structures for the Teichmüller tower.
transcription_corrections: '(resp. l'orientation et les structures toriques)' should read '(respectant l'orientation et les structures toriques)'.
The NB line probably reads 'SUT(X) ≃ T(X) ×_{S_I} Aut((T_i)_{i∈I})' (fiber product over S_I).
'SRT^!(X) = R^I . S_*T^!(X)' is annotated 'noyau de SRT^!(X) → S_I', i.e. SRT^! is defined as the kernel of SRT(X) → S_I.
In the base-point paragraph, the group is likely 'S_*T(X,s)' (non-pure, with permutations), not 'S_*T^!(X,s)'; the exclamation mark appears crossed or altered in the image.
'chaque fois qu'on donne une [?] orig.' is likely 'chaque fois qu'on se donne une origine', i.e. a point s_i on each T_i.
